habitat: Damp grassland, woodland, meadows and rocky places
blurb: Upright stems of nodding blue-purple bells over neat ladder-like pinnate leaves — the classic cottage-garden Jacob's ladder for a shady, reliably moist corner. Worth knowing that despite its place on CSU's native list, this species is a Eurasian one.
water: Moderate — steady moisture in part shade; not a xeric plant
spread: Upright clumping; self-sows modestly in moist shade
seasons: Blue-purple bell flowers in summer over ladder-like pinnate foliage; dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists it as plantable to about 9,000 ft. It is hardy well past anything Boulder produces; the limit here is heat and dryness rather than cold.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade — the one plant in this group that genuinely wants organic matter and shelter rather than grit and sun.[1][3]
care.water: Moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–18 in wide. Clusters of bell-shaped flowers on upright plants over small pinnately compound leaves.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August; CSU records the colour as blue, purple and the height as 18–24 in tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: **A nativity note, stated plainly.** CSU's fact sheet 7.242 lists this plant among Colorado natives, but *Polemonium caeruleum* is native to temperate Europe and northern Asia. Colorado's own Jacob's ladders are the western *P. occidentale* and the towering *P. foliosissimum*; some treatments sink the former into *P. caeruleum* as a subspecies, which is the likeliest reason for the listing. This guide therefore badges it **Non-native** with its honest Eurasian origin. If you specifically want the native, ask a nursery for *P. foliosissimum* or *P. occidentale*.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

references.name: CSU Extension — Native Herbaceous Perennials for Colorado Landscapes (fact sheet 7.242, PDF: complete Table 1)

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the authorities consulted; grown as a shade ornamental.[1][3]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for Jacob's ladder, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. It has an old herbal record under the name Greek valerian, but a folk-medicinal history is not a food record and carries no dosing guidance, so it is not presented as either here.[1][3]
